📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the morning of 4 December 2024, the Los Angeles-based artist Stanya Kahn opened X (formerly Twitter) to get her daily news digest, when she, like many Americans, was inundated with a mass chorus of tweets—ranging from celebratory snark to unbridled vitriol—about the assassination of United HealthCare’s chief executive Brian Thompson.

In a recent development, “The compression of anger and joy that I was seeing people write that day was astonishing,” Kahn tells The Art Newspaper; she immediately felt compelled to capture the torrent of reactions. “At first I was bookmarking them, and then [screenshotting] them, and fairly swiftly my thought was to gather these up because the algorithm might start shutting them down.”.

Industry observers note that fairly quickly, the Trump administration declared that any celebration of the killing could be criminalised. But with an ever-growing archive and a long-held practice as a time-based media artist, Kahn decided to create a film that chronologically presented the public’s rapidly unfolding response to this now-infamous event.

Flyer for Deny, Defend, Depose (2026) Courtesy of Stanya Kahn.

Titled Deny Defend Depose (2026)—a play on the words scrawled on three shell casings from bullets fired in the shooting, and the strategy invoked by major healthcare providers to reduce payouts and increase profits—Kahn’s film is now screening across the country at artist-run-spaces, cinemas and galleries. The Fresh York non-profit space Participant Inc will screen it on 13 November, with more showings to come.

According to recent reports, originally, Kahn planned to release the film in the lead-up to 9 September, when the state trial of Luigi Mangione was due to take place in Latest York. Now that Mangione’s 14 August guilty plea—an attempt to avoid double jeopardy—has postponed the state hearing until 10 December, with a federal hearing to follow on 18 December, Kahn plans to continue updating the film with more responses from the public as the saga continues.

It has been revealed that when it all began, she had considered turning the project into a coffee-table book, which would afford a funny inversion of X’s quippy, short-form format. But switching to a film, her primary medium, afforded an opportunity for in-person film screenings, which enabled the originally solitary experience of watching the commentary unfold online to be transformed into a collective viewing experience.

Stanya Kahn, Deny, Defend, Depose (2026, still), 30:28 min Courtesy of the artist.

In a recent development, set to a dramatic soundtrack of acid and jungle, the 30-minute film takes viewers on an emotional rollercoaster. Watching the tweets unfold in sequence together, the audience collectively holds its breadth as anticipation builds to the moment the suspect is revealed as Mangione, laughs as tweets comment on his attractiveness or the Monopoly money found in his backpack, and sighs at the devastating state of healthcare in the United States when statistics regarding industry salaries and investment patterns, or personal anecdotes about life-threatening denials, are shared.

Just like Kahn was glued to X that morning in late 2024, viewers of her film are often transfixed as they relive their reactions to the still-unfolding story at top speed.“The poignancy of such a broad spectrum of the American public responding in kind to what was basically a public political assassination felt like a rupture, especially in party-based politics,” Kahn says. “It cut across the entire political spectrum and the common ground that suddenly emerged in this flashpoint seemed like a new beacon for potential mass movement, because it was a unity that emerged spontaneously and instantaneously, it wasn’t something that got hammered out in time.”.

The outpouring of affection for Mangione has been staggering, Kahn says. “Without blinking,” she adds, “people were in full-throat applause of [an alleged] murderer.”.

Stanya Kahn, Deny, Defend, Depose (2026, still), 30:28 min Courtesy of the artist.

Attention from the media and public has remained steady since the early days of the manhunt, Mangione’s arrest and the trial, with comparisons to Robin Hood, lookalike contests and wanted posters for other healthcare company executives. While the extent of the public’s celebration of Thompson’s killing took many by surprise, Kahn sees this reaction as evidence of just “how deep the pain and anger and frustration is in this country about the evilness of the healthcare system and its inaccessibility”. (Per capita spending on healthcare in the US is double the average of other wealthy countries, and has been increasing faster than inflation for decades.).

Thompson’s killing and its aftermath are hardly a black-and-white tale of righteous moral vengeance. Though some originally attempted to paint Mangione as disaffected and radicalised, his Ivy League education and privileged upbringing told a different story. And the responses to the event “weren’t just coming from more radical spaces”, Kahn indicates. While capturing their reactions in real time and reviewing the posters’ profiles, she found, “it was literally just ‘every man’—people with five followers and five million. It was regular people because they were pissed.”.

#57261. The Power of Kindness in a World Driven by Probability

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1129 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

The Power of Kindness in a World Driven by Probability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • "We place life’s bets by countless calculations of probability, conscious and unconscious, only to discover over and over how short they fall of the wildest reaches of the possible, which always includes but exceeds the probable." —Maria Popova.
  • “I’ve been searching for ways to heal myself, and I’ve found that kindness is the best way.” —Lady Gaga.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

"We place life’s bets by countless calculations of probability, conscious and unconscious, only to discover over and over how short they fall of the wildest reaches of the possible, which always includes but exceeds the probable." —Maria Popova.

“I’ve been searching for ways to heal myself, and I’ve found that kindness is the best way.” —Lady Gaga.

In a recent development, "The question is not: what have I achieved? But rather: who can I be when I am with you? Who can you be when you are with me?" —Nora Bateson.

It has been revealed that we live in a world, at least in our hectic Western-based culture, that is driven by probability. What is probability? How does it taste, smell, or feel? Does it just linger in our complexity, waiting for a never-achieved form? We calculate within probability both with our awareness and unawareness. It penetrates our educational, economic, political, and medical systems. It assumes that we will automatically accept models of certainty. Yet our problems still exist in the domain of probable content.

Industry observers note that probability is all-powerful and designed to make you believe its outcomes are absolute. It waits for our lives to pass through it with definitive rules to fit all. However, it can never seem to guarantee success. It tries to be the basis of caution, yet it can also be the source of the other side of safety. It can, in many instances, be the origin of violence and discrimination.

It has been revealed that why? Probability measures the likelihood or chance that a specific event will occur. It survives on unresolved paradoxes of this or that, and that misses the yin/yang, messy/beautifulness of life in all its complexity. It can be funny, as in humor, and puzzling with choices, but when not harnessed, it feels separate and fragmented, avoiding the ecological process of how all patterns connect.

Industry observers note that probability evades the wisdom of understanding how love, altruism, and empathy can breed kindness, which some might consider the regulating homeostasis basis of living systems. Anthropologist Gregory Bateson more than hinted at the misunderstanding of probability’s faults by suggesting that absolute outcomes hide how "Human actions involve play, context, and the probability of disaster or risk within a relationship." Probability makes us too busy to savor what happens between relationships, yet when we do, it can help us step back from absolute outcomes and certainty and find improvisational potential. When we do, with encouragement, this can create all kinds of possibilities. Maria Popova, for instance, mentions in the first stanza of her poem "The Wildest Bet Is the Winning Bet":.

"You wouldn’t have bet on it,the battered rockorbiting a starfrom the discount binof the universe".

Probability dissolves when you zoom outward with your personal lens and widen your perspective, making room for kindness to be born. Probability, in this case, begins to blend with how we share our possessions. It becomes an advocate for tending to others' needs, which gives ultimate meaning to who we are as humans. It becomes the terrain of kindness, the quality or state of being friendly, generous, considerate, and genuinely concerned for the well-being of others. Through kindness, we can choose to blend with the paradoxes inherent in unchecked probability to see an ecological unity in a manner felt by C.S. Lewis, who wrote in Surprised by Joy: "Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else—whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard—does the 'thrill' arise." That is the prerequisite for kindness.

Recent findings suggest that using kindness as an ecological framework supports a sense of order in contrast to probability’s search for finite answers. This demand for finitude is what excludes kindness because it depends on producing outcomes. Kindness, however, is driven by understanding the constraints and interdependency of any living system. This is why it is woven into global popular symbolism and metaphors. It is based on maintaining what may be good for humanity rather than accumulating something. It is forming a kinship based on forgiveness, not to condone past pain but to move forward with altruism and empathy. Kindness emerges in what poet Allen Ginsberg poetically called a state that "stretches thru every probability." It is the beginner's mind of temporary emptiness, which can at first seem conceptually liable, mistaken for sheer nothingness, yet is in fact the improvisational potential for possibilities of kindness.

According to recent reports, we must recognize this need for kindness, especially in today's struggle to accept diversity. This underscores a profound reminder, particularly useful as we celebrate Thanksgiving, that the Anglo experience in North America began as a massive mistake in probability, as Garrison Keillor reminds us: "...we survived only by the kindness of strangers who had every reason to be cruel." In a quote often attributed to Mark Twain, this type of innate empathy is "...the language which the deaf can hear and the blind can see.".

When the dictates of probability, with seemingly good intentions, succumb to the dark side of fragmented content in our educational systems, isolated profit-driven health mandates, and sociopolitical polarization, the antidote is massive acts of kindness. This releases feel-good neurotransmitters like dopamine, serotonin, and endorphins. It activates the brain's reward center, creating euphoria and emotional warmth. It further reduces stress by soothing the vagus nerve, which recharges and rejuvenates when it feels secure.

Industry observers note that it is interesting how unchecked probability is the cloak of "science" that constantly tries to quantify or refute the effects of kindness, when it only needs to observe how it strengthens social bonds like a welcome adhesive. Kindness can increase trust and collaboration, and encourage greater equity in the distribution of wealth, security, and opportunity, allowing for our innate interdependency with each other and nature. Another worthwhile attribute is the resulting togetherness that correlates with lower rates of anxiety and depression. Consider this in contrast to the array of physical ailments that can occur with unchecked probability, and it's a choice worth exploring.

Here are some prompts to help you sustain kindness as an antidote to probability. Use them with someone else or in groups. After each response, follow up with at least five “How did that affect you?” questions and ask how you can make a difference. Then discuss using paraphrasing to provide feedback about what was heard.

Bateson, Gregory. "A Theory of Play and Fantasy." In Steps to an Ecology of Mind: Collected Essays in Anthropology, Psychiatry, Evolution, and Epistemology, 177–193. San Francisco: Chandler Publishing Firm, 1972.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Dinner Ladies needed a recipe for a rebrand that would not only pay respect to their unique origin story but bring their visual and verbal identity up to speed with their growth as Australia’s tastiest frozen meal service. We joined forces to cook them up a fresh look and feel that reflects their homely meals and anti-“mumsy” attitude, extending all the way from their website through to their packaging. Now whack the oven on, because Australia’s hottest frozen meal service has arrived.

In a recent development, since it all began with two determined women in a Sydney-side backyard shed in 2007, The Dinner Ladies have been filling the freezers, bellies and hearts of thousands of busy Australian families with their ready-to-heat comfort meals. Born from a deep understanding of dinner time chaos, and the desire to bring some ease back into this routine, The Dinner Ladies’ commitment to delivering meals worthy of mum’s tick of approval remains unwavering.

Sources indicate that the market for pre-prepared meal delivery is an oversaturated landscape steeped in clichés and same-same messaging that claims to be the most healthy, convenient or delicious dinnertime solution. They not only lack a distinct personality but also relatability to their customer — time-poor people who just want simple, genuinely good, homemade meals that help take the pressure off when it’s needed most. This is where The Dinner Ladies shine. A flavour-stacked service that takes care of dinner, so you can focus on doing life.

Sources indicate that the brand had become known and loved for their unexpected, no nonsense and slightly audacious approach. This was not only refreshingly real but a reflection of both their wholesome offering and the founding ladies. However, over seventeen years of brand iterations their look had become diluted, lost its attitudinal punch, and needed a major serve of reinvigoration. Our vision was to bring back the best from their history and turn up the heat across the board to let the nation know they mean (meal delivery) business.

We fully immersed ourselves in The Dinner Ladies story, from taking a deep dive through past website designs and hand drawn logos on a napkin, to visiting the shed where it all began and the factory where it now thrives. This helped us draw out the strongest existing brand elements, like their early trad-tattoo-esque illustrations and counter-“mumsy” stereotype, and turn them into a modern evolution. Driven by “Food from the Heart,” each component of the visual identity communicates the brand essence and no-BS confidence of a service that truly helps take the stress out of dinnertime.

In a recent development, the first step was the refinement of the logo. By decoupling the heart and the script, we gave it flexibility, made it easier to read at every touchpoint and allowed it to scale as needed. The custom heart logo was designed by us and then, alongside the wordmark, handed to illustrator Jake Foreman to redraw and personalise with his iconic texture and gritty stipple.

In a recent development, the Dinner Ladies’ existing red already had distinct brand attribution in the category so we just refined it with a bright and modern twist. The secondary palette supports our hero red with a balance of warm, approachable and slightly retro hues. When united, the system unlocks a number of interesting and vibrant combinations that are particularly useful across hard-working digital applications.

We used the typeface Denim by Displaay Type Foundry to show off the brand’s confident personality yet retain practicality. Denim Wide’s used in headings and call-to-action applications to command attention, while its regular cut counterpart rounds out the system with a friendly, clean and legible option for subheadings and body copy. With its subtle details, the typeface can be an attention-grabbing hero element that showcases the bold tone of voice but also work alongside more expressive moments.

In a recent development, the tone of voice needed to capture the brand’s joyful, cheeky yet comforting personality, while steering clear of any patronising “mumsy” tropes and stereotypes. We worked with copywriter Cat Wall to develop a verbal identity that balanced the empathetic caregiver with the charmingly rebellious tone of the ladies themselves. In a category saturated with over-sincerity and fake friendliness, the tone offers a refreshing sprinkle of irreverence with a straight-forward, bull-free reflection of the audience and their needs.

It has been revealed that the photography celebrates the authentic messiness of real life dinnertime. A reflection of the brand’s tell-it-like-it-is attitude, the shoot didn’t shy away from capturing raw moments — the remnants of a great dish alongside a latest one being served or a bolognese-faced baby — mixed with the joy of sharing generous, mouth-watering food.

It has been revealed that with Alana Dimou behind the lens, Jerrie-Joy Redman-Lloyd on styling, Oriana De Luca on wardrobe, Gavin Anesbury with a hair and makeup brush in hand, and Michaela Le on production, the brand came to life. Warm, natural lighting, combined with quirky styling choices, pops of colour or pattern and intentional (and encouraged) chaos set a homely and inviting scene with a pinch of rebellion.

Illustration has always been a major piece of The Dinner Ladies’ brand so we wanted to bring it across to the rebrand. The original illustrations’ punk and rough-around-the-edges flair drew us to references of traditional trad tattoos.

In a recent development, collaborating further with illustrator Jake Foreman, we crafted a suite of illustrations that served as both personality-rich storytelling pieces and functional devices. While the small scenes and spots speak to specific offerings of the brand, the hero illustration speaks to the love behind every Dinner Ladies dish and the comforting shared experiences created around the table.

These illustrations are supported by our suite of type-furniture elements that not only support the main design elements but add character to any layout.

In a recent development, as a product that’s often shoved into the freezer and then reached for in a rush, legibility and easy differentiation were priorities for designing the packaging. A simple colour-coded system helps to distinguish between protein groups at a glance, making it quick and effortless to find the crowd-pleasing meal that’s ready to save the day.

The Dinner Ladies now have a brand that not only celebrates their seventeen year legacy but gives them the tools for future decades of success. The flexible design system and punchy tone of voice pays tribute to their tenacious past, the founding ladies behind the service and their wholesome mission put joy back into dinner time. Now The Dinner Ladies can stand loud and proud with a brand that reflects their readiness to dish up delicious dinners to an entire nation.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BOND builds the Aleph Farms brand identity from a single flipped letter for cultivated meat: the ancient aleph, turned over, becomes an ox.

BOND calls it turning steak on its head. Cultivated meat is one of the most significant developments in food production in generations, and the studio treats it as a story about continuity, not the future. Aleph Farms grows meat directly from animal cells, without raising or slaughtering animals, and BOND was asked to build both the parent brand and its first consumer product brand, Aleph Cuts. The name comes from the first letter of one of humanity's oldest writing systems, first drawn as the pictogram of an ox, and the identity took Gold at the European Design Awards in 2024.

The wordmark does the talking. Aleph Farms reads in a sturdy grotesque, white on a deep green field, with the flipped letter tucked into a circle as the mark, the ox reappearing as a small geometric head. Aleph Cuts gets a different voice entirely: soft, rounded, almost liquid letterforms in dark green on coral, the same ox mark sitting beside it. The parent brand is the steady statement, the product brand is the appetite.

It has been revealed that the flip is the organising principle of the whole system. BOND runs it through typography, motion, imagery, and communication, so every panel reads as one argument. The palette stays tight: deep green, coral, and pale blue against off-white, with the ox mark repeating at every scale, from card to plate. The parent brand and the product brand keep distinct roles while sharing the same idea and visual language.

The material language is quiet and tactile. Business cards carry the mark blind debossed into dark green and white stock, the circle and the ox pressed into the paper rather than printed on it. The same mark is pressed into the center of a plate, a small stamped seal in the middle of an empty dish, waiting for the food. Nothing shouts. The identity holds its nerve and lets the mark do the work.

Julia Stotz photographs the food the way the brand thinks. A skewer comes off a smoking grill against a dark green backdrop, sliced steak stacks on a white plate with mushrooms and peppers, and the meat stays the subject, never a prop. The photography keeps the palette of the system, green backdrops, pale cloth, so the product shots sit inside the identity, not next to it. The result is a brand for something that never existed before that still looks like it has always been at the table.

Philadelphia city council investigates sudden closure of oldest natural history research institution in the Americas

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Academy of Natural Sciences, a 198-year-old public museum in Philadelphia run by Drexel University, shuttered in September because of rising costs.
  • In a recent development, while many of the Academy’s workers have been laid off, collection managers still on staff have faced an “astronomical increase” in emails and calls, notes Amber Redfield, a former geosciences collection manager and fossil preparator at the Academy who was recently laid off and is now volunteering there.
  • Isa Betancourt, a former curatorial assistant in the entomology department and an organiser with the Save the Academy coalition, says the number of curators has dropped from 11 to five.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Academy of Natural Sciences, a 198-year-old public museum in Philadelphia run by Drexel University, shuttered in September because of rising costs. The university’s president will now testify under subpoena before Philadelphia’s city council on 16 November, answering questions about the sudden closure and what will happen to the museum’s valuable collection of more than 19 million specimens.

In a recent development, while many of the Academy’s workers have been laid off, collection managers still on staff have faced an “astronomical increase” in emails and calls, notes Amber Redfield, a former geosciences collection manager and fossil preparator at the Academy who was recently laid off and is now volunteering there. She says that people have been asking: “Is this safe?” “Can I see it?” “Can I book an appointment?”.

Isa Betancourt, a former curatorial assistant in the entomology department and an organiser with the Save the Academy coalition, says the number of curators has dropped from 11 to five. The invertebrate palaeontology collection manager recently left for a job at the American Museum of Natural History. “There is no plan to replace her," Betancourt tells The Art Newspaper. Endowed curator posts in entomology and palaeontology have gone unfilled for years, she adds.

Founded in 1812, the Academy describes itself as the oldest natural history research institution in the Americas. It opened its museum to the public in 1828 and, in 1868, put Hadrosaurus foulkii on view as the world’s first mounted dinosaur skeleton. Its millions of specimens include plants collected on the Lewis and Clark expedition, John James Audubon’s birds and Thomas Jefferson’s fossils.

The Academy became a Drexel affiliate in 2011, while retaining its status as a separate non-profit with its own board. Drexel recently told the city council it had “stepped in as a partner” that year, when the Academy “faced severe financial distress”.

The city council passed a resolution on 17 September to investigate the Academy’s closing. The resolution calls institutions like the Academy “part of the cultural fabric of the city” and says its shuttering would especially affect area residents “for whom the museum is a fixture of the neighbourhood”. An initial hearing took place on 26 October, which Drexel’s president did not attend.

At the hearing, representatives for Drexel cited the building's "substantial capital needs" and told the city council that public exhibitions need a upcoming model, "almost certainly in a different location".

Sarah McAnulty, a squid biologist and Save the Academy organiser, claims city council members asked Drexel representatives to check their numbers. "If all you need to keep the public museum open is a million dollars, what the hell are we doing here?" she says, describing the city council’s reaction.

The Academy’s Dinosaur Hall Photo: Ms3733, via Wikimedia Commons.

It has been revealed that staff learned of the Academy’s closure at a morning meeting on 1 September, Redfield says. Most staff were laid off by 1 November, and many people "found out they were let go in a report by The Philadelphia Inquirer", she adds.

Redfield says the museum drew more than 60,000 visitors in its final 12 days of public hours. "That's not enough time to shut down a lifetime of scientific and educational work," she adds. "I planned to retire at the Academy and don't have any backup intends." Now she is volunteering.

"Unfortunately, volunteer labour is essential to most natural history collections, but it’s not sustainable,” Betancourt states. “The fact that the volunteer manager was initially slated for termination and had to be reinstated shows Drexel has no idea how these collections function.".

Betancourt adds that the Academy's social media accounts have been inactive for two months and staff do not have access because Drexel controls them. The Academy's director of marketing and communications was let go with the closure. Betancourt notes the university may not realise that communications and education staff connect the collections with the public and potential benefactors, "otherwise, the collections work in darkness”.

According to recent reports, the William Penn Foundation has offered a year of funding to replace Drexel's subsidy for the museum. "The foundation has not received a response to our offer," a spokesperson told the Inquirer. Drexel later stated that it had not received a "formal proposal with a defined level of financial support".

Betancourt notes Save the Academy wants Drexel to explain "why no capital campaign was undertaken" and "why the scientific community has been shut out of behind-the-scenes negotiations. The closed-door negotiations got us a closed museum. Natural history collections tied to a financially haemorrhaging university are not safe natural history collections.”.

Friday Five With Shaina Tabak: Art, Architecture, and the Spaces Between

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that though she’s still pursuing her MFA in Visual Arts at Columbia University, artist Shaina Tabak is hardly a newcomer to the art world.
  • Tabak’s own work is equally expansive.
  • ‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that though she’s still pursuing her MFA in Visual Arts at Columbia University, artist Shaina Tabak is hardly a newcomer to the art world. The RISD graduate, who earned her BFA in furniture design, already has more than 20 exhibitions under her belt. Now she’s adding curator to her résumé with 260 Madison, an artist-run exhibition bringing together more than 50 artists across a former Duane Reade storefront and a 23,000-square-foot office floor above it in Midtown Manhattan.

Tabak’s own work is equally expansive. Drawing on history, technology, and materiality, she explores the relationship between the digital and physical worlds, often starting with digitally modeled forms that she translates into sculptures through hands-on processes such as cutting, perforation, lamination, and extrusion.

‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

But her interest in materials extends beyond their physical properties. She also sees them as records of labor, manufacturing, extraction, and use. Her work examines contemporary material culture through a historical lens, imagining how the things made and valued today might be understood generations from now. As she puts it, her sculptures are “less concerned with imagining the future than with creating historical distance from the present.”.

In a recent development, that perspective comes through in her recent work, which examines the increasingly blurred line between looking and shopping. In her Brooklyn studio, the Queens-born artist has been embedding collected industrial objects in three-ply cardboard, referencing the packaging and shipping systems that support consumer culture. She’s also exploring the influence of visual search and algorithmic commerce, where objects spotted in an image can lead to an endless stream of purchasable alternatives. It’s a commentary on a culture in which images don’t just inspire desire; they generate transactions.

‘First Water (deer)’ and ‘First Water (banner)’ (2026) by Dexter Barker-Glenn on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

For today’s Friday Five, we spent five minutes with Shaina Tabak to explore the ideas behind her curatorial debut at 260 Madison and the influences shaping her own work in the exhibition.

‘Ghosts’ (2025) by Alisa Berger and ‘Impaler Shield’ (2026) by Kari Cholnoky on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

It has been revealed that for her curatorial debut, Tabak drew on Columbia University’s MFA community and her own network of artists, bringing together emerging talents and established names. Co-curated by artistic duo Dayana Matasheva and Edson Niebla Rodríguez of Demon Lovers, Inc., 260 Madison includes artists such as Simon Denny, Jon Kessler, and Eva and Franco Mattes. The exhibition was organized in collaboration with the building’s owner, AmTrustRE, which gave the curators full creative control.

‘Longcat’ (2026) by Eva & Franco Mattes on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

On view through Nov. 22, 2026, the expansive exhibition brings together familiar materials, objects, and technologies that are dismantled, reconstructed, or made strange. Exposed HVAC, ripped-out toilets, and corporate-logo wallpaper create the backdrop for works spanning sculpture, upcoming media, and video. Tabak’s goal for 260 Madison is to “examine the systems organizing contemporary life—from control, surveillance, AI, and extraction to the material and architectural structures that shape how we work, move, and live.”.

Below, in her own words, Tabak shares the influences that shaped her approach to 260 Madison, from artist-run exhibitions that challenged traditional institutions to architectural theories and sculptures that informed her own work.

Shaina Tabak’s works ‘Localized Collapse / Frozen Zone’ (2026) and ‘Sweep Towards Skylight’ (2026) on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of the artist.

Sources indicate that “The first one, Damien Hirst’s Freeze (1988), was suggested to me by my professor Jon Kessler. Freeze was particularly compelling because it took place amid the redevelopment of London’s Docklands and was itself supported by real-estate developers, revealing the uneasy relationship between artistic independence and the production of urban capital. That history made me particularly conscious of a contradiction in our own project: While 260 Madison temporarily interrupts the building’s commercial function, the exhibition also generates cultural value for a property undergoing modernization.”.

“A more recent exhibition, Christopher Wool’s See Stop Run (2024), took place in Fresh York City’s Financial District and demonstrated how artists could operate outside established institutions by appropriating vacant commercial spaces. Wool’s exhibition was also installed on a gutted office floor and offered a more immediate architectural reference, allowing the building’s exposed infrastructure and traces of demolition to enter into dialogue with the work. With 260 Madison, we wanted to push these precedents even further, treating the vacant corporate office as a material record of changing relationships between labor, capital, and the built environment.”.

Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

According to recent reports, “Rem Koolhaas’ book Delirious Upcoming York and his essay “Junkspace” were really helpful in connecting the architecture of the space to the exhibition. My partner has worked on the 17th floor of 260 Madison for the past three years—a complete coincidence—and his 9-to-5 job as a paralegal brought to mind Koolhaas’ concepts of the vertical schism, architectural lobotomy, and definitive instability as I considered the exhibition’s function.”.

“All three of Koolhaas’ concepts, in their own ways, describe the Manhattan skyscraper as a structure in which the exterior remains independent of the interior, allowing different floors to accommodate radically different and constantly changing activities without altering the building’s outward appearance.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I was thinking about House, a temporary public sculpture by Rachel Whiteread, when creating my sculpture Swept Towards Skylight (2026) for 260 Madison. I embedded an earlier work in insulation foam and coated it with cement to give the illusion that the negative space around it had been cast solid. Whiteread’s work transformed the interior of a house slated for demolition into a concrete monument to its former inhabitants and the lives that had occupied it.”.

Industry observers note that “I kept returning to this idea while curating 260 Madison, where the vacant office floor still bears physical traces of the labor and routines that once animated it. I wanted the building to function not simply as a container for artworks, but as an artifact in its own right, with its exposed infrastructure and signs of abandonment becoming part of the exhibition. What interests me about House, and what I hoped to capture at 260 Madison, was how architecture outlives its function and becomes a monument to the systems that once gave it meaning.”.

260 Madison is on view through Nov. 22, 2026, at 260 Madison Avenue in New York City.

A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the last century or so, ever since wood fell out of style, the bodies of most automobiles have been made from a few tried-and-true materials: carbon fiber, fiberglass, aluminum, and steel, with the metals proving most popular.
  • But what if you didn’t have to worry about such concerns?
  • “It was a proposal I made to the client, Carlos Peralta,” Giugiaro says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the last century or so, ever since wood fell out of style, the bodies of most automobiles have been made from a few tried-and-true materials: carbon fiber, fiberglass, aluminum, and steel, with the metals proving most popular. The choices are a balancing act, forcing carmakers to weigh price, safety, convenience, and appearance to determine which substance makes the most sense for the masses.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

But what if you didn’t have to worry about such concerns? What if cost was no object, practicality a formality, and there was no need to cater to the wants of more than one owner? Well, that was the lucky circumstance designer Fabrizio Giugiaro, founder and CEO of GFG Style, found himself in when creating the Peralta D, a gran turismo with a body made of hand-hammered copper.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

“It was a proposal I made to the client, Carlos Peralta,” Giugiaro says. The duo had worked together before on the design house’s first one-off automobile, the spitshine-polished 1980s-esque Peralta S. For the follow-up, Giugiaro wanted to draw a deeper connection to the owner. As an industrialist, Peralta has business interests involving copper, so Giugiaro suggested it as the material.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Recent findings suggest that giugiaro’s name is well known in the automotive world. His father, Giorgetto Giugiaro, is a master of clean-line designs—he penned the DeLorean DMC-12, the BMW M1, the original Lotus Esprit, and the first Volkswagen Golf. The senior Giugiaro’s career has included work for Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bugatti, and many more of the world’s most notable automotive brands. The father-and-son duo founded GFG Style together over a decade ago, but it’s only been in recent years that they’ve been dedicating their talents to bespoke coachbuilt cars for individual collectors, as with the Peralta D.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

And while using copper for a car’s bodywork may be unorthodox, the designer notes it wasn’t as difficult as it may seem. “It really surprised us that copper proved to be much more malleable than the aluminum we had worked with previously; it is also considerably easier to weld and polish,” Fabrizio says. “Of course, it does come with the disadvantage of greater weight, but since it was combined with a supporting structure made entirely of carbon fiber, the overall balance between the materials ultimately worked out well.”.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Beneath all that copper lies the chassis of a 2025 Maserati GranTurismo Trofeo—itself a stylish design, but one far removed from the almost brutalist simplicity of the Peralta D’s angles. Instead of traditional doors, the car features a dramatic opening system inspired by the Peralta S’s single-motion dome, with independently opening side windows and gullwing-style openings at the rear to access the back seats.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Industry observers note that inside, copper-colored leather adorns most surfaces, broken up (almost) only by the infotainment and dashboard screens, which offer some of the few hints of its Maserati roots. Meant to showcase the bond between its owner and his daughters, the car comes with a few (perhaps stereotypically) female-oriented features, such as a passenger-side makeup station with an illuminated mirror and dedicated cosmetic storage. And while the rear seats are tight, a retractable refrigerator designed to hold a bottle of champagne and four copper glasses means occupants can easily distract themselves.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

While the Peralta D might seem to push the boundaries—or at least the materials—of road-going automobile design to their limits, Fabrizio suggests even wilder builds may follow in its tire tracks.

“I have another alternative material in mind, one that has only ever been used once before,” he says, “so it will be another surprise…”.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Will Sabel Courtney has been working in journalism since 2010, specializing primarily in automotive and men’s lifestyle writing. He has driven too many cars to count over the course of his career. A native of Vermont, he has lived in New York City for two decades, dividing his time between Manhattan and Brooklyn, where he now resides.

#57254. Tech Report: Comment | Is art market regulation too much of a ‘good thing’?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (679 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Comment | Is art market regulation too much of a ‘good thing’?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (679 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that anyone who states the art market is unregulated probably has not spent much time in an auction house compliance department.
  • In the European Union (EU) and UK, this includes regulation around money-laundering, data protection, imports and exports, artist resale rights, a growing economic sanctions regime, endangered species, firearms and complex tax reporting.
  • None of these areas of control seem objectionable at first glance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that anyone who states the art market is unregulated probably has not spent much time in an auction house compliance department. At the major houses, such departments might consist of half a dozen full-time personnel tasked with ensuring that the business can digest what has become an expanding layer cake of government regulation in the art sector.

In the European Union (EU) and UK, this includes regulation around money-laundering, data protection, imports and exports, artist resale rights, a growing economic sanctions regime, endangered species, firearms and complex tax reporting. The UK has additional obligations around ivory and issuing annual “modern slavery” statements.

None of these areas of control seem objectionable at first glance. But a careful observer must consider two things. Does the imposition of regulation achieve the intended goal? And, if it does, does it need to apply across the board, both up and down the market, to all participants?

Recent findings suggest that in 2015, the British Art Market Federation undertook an analysis that listed 167 laws and regulations impacting the UK art market. The organisation’s current chair, Tom Christopherson, tells me that the impact of laws and regulations has increased considerably since then. Sophisticated players, with their compliance teams and in-house lawyers, may be able to spot trends, change course and avoid falling foul of the many rules. But what about the small fish?

Consider anti-money laundering regulations, which were extended to the art market by the EU and the UK in 2020. Absolutely nobody wants ill-gotten gains to proliferate in the art market. But despite negative stereotypes and hearsay around “dodgy dealings”, I have yet to find convincing evidence of money laundering in the European art market that could have justified such an expansive regime.

Recent findings suggest that in the UK, data from HMRC (the official tax, payments, and customs authority) shows that more than 200 art market participants have been fined for violating the rules from the date enforcement began in 2022 to September 2025. None of these infractions involved the actual laundering of money, merely the failure to register with HMRC or to report material changes. (One gallery failed on additional grounds relating to risk assessments, due diligence and staff training.) Many of those fined are small operations, such as a toy soldier shop in London that featured in a recent Financial Times story on this topic.

Sources indicate that with registration and reporting obligations, the onus falls on market participants. The scope of an offence can extend well beyond laundering itself. With the art market now a “regulated sector”, failure to report suspicions around, for instance, activities that could conceivably be connected to the funding of terrorism is now a criminal offence. An east London art dealer was caught under this newly introduced “failure to report” offence in 2023 and sentenced to two-and-a-half years behind bars.

It has been revealed that another area involves sanctions, far less simple than checking customer names against a list of oligarchs. The Russia sanctions list continues to grow by the month; in the UK, it consists of nearly 2,000 individuals and 1,000 companies—with additional lists for countries including Belarus, Iran and Libya—often with a multitude of transliterated names.

Recent findings suggest that also in the UK, an offence exists that goes beyond dealing with listed sanctioned individuals to exporting or “making available” luxury goods (including art) to anyone “connected with Russia”. This offence was used recently to charge the gallery Hauser & Wirth, along with its shipping firm. Judge Tony Baumgartner of Southwark Crown Court dismissed the case in July, having found that the prosecution had failed to make a case that the individual to whom the work had been shipped was indeed “connected with Russia”, as he was no longer ordinarily residing in that country.

Sources indicate that we all understand the benefit of regulation when it comes to saving lives, protecting the environment and smothering criminality in high-risk markets. But whether every piece of regulation is justified for the art world remains to be seen—or, rather, proven.

Recent findings suggest that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Recent findings suggest that here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

According to recent reports, the annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:.

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

It has been revealed that this is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

Recent findings suggest that when you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — at the moment $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

It has been revealed that let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

According to recent reports, at the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

One of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 strategy for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Sources indicate that example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

The current $13.61 million lifetime exemption is scheduled to drop to approximately $7 million per person on January 1, 2026. For high-net-worth families, this creates a narrow window to transfer wealth at the higher exemption level. If you have a taxable estate anywhere near the future threshold, consult an estate planning attorney about accelerating gifts before the sunset takes effect.

A practical guide to making gifts without triggering tax.

Give up to $18,000 per recipient per year with no reporting, no forms, and no impact on your lifetime exemption. Married couples can give $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

Payments made directly to educational institutions or medical providers for someone else are unlimited and completely excluded from gift tax. These do not reduce your annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single person, file IRS Form 709 with your tax return. The excess reduces your $13.61 million lifetime exemption but no tax is owed until you exceed it.

The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hybrid and remote work have changed what people expect from a modern workspace. No longer do people want fixed seating or single-purpose design. Instead, they are looking for modular, multi-use furniture that boosts productivity while maintaining comfort and style. When Chris and Jon Panichella set out to design their latest seating collection for Arcadia, they turned to everyday life for inspiration.

“The idea for Almeya began with a woman working from an inflatable raft at the beach,” the Panichellas explain. “She could recline and read in one position, then sit up and work in another—a simple moment that captured how much people now expect from their spaces: comfort, flexibility, and function. That observation became the very first concept sketch that eventually evolved into the Almeya offering we know today.”.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

Recent findings suggest that with a full family of products—including modular, lounge, work-lounge, benches, and occasional tables—the Almeya Collection offers a fluid experience that adapts to these modern shifts in productivity and collaboration. Across the series, soft, organic forms invite comfort and ease, while integrated tables, flexible configurations, and strategic power stations allow for both focus and sociability.

Almeya began with a single lounge chair and an integrated two-tiered side table. The idea was simple: the combination could function as a self-contained work island, with two separate surfaces, power access, and an optional rotating tablet. With this concept in mind, the Panichellas developed a standalone lounge chair, love seat, and sofa with the same flexible spirit. (Case in point: The swivel-base lounge chair allows for adaptability and easy collaboration). Finally, the complete collection came together, designed to support the various—and often unpredictable—ways people work and gather.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

Industry observers note that to inspire interaction, designers are encouraged to group lounge seating intermittently to foster spontaneous connections. To create pathways or natural flow within a space, they can explore Almeya’s modular capabilities. The organic curves of the lounge models also create an inviting warmth, blurring the line between contract and residential. And for healthcare and education settings, optional clean-outs are offered between the seat and back.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

Completing the collection, occasional tables carry the same gentle, organic language for a cohesive experience. Available in multiple sizes and shapes, tables feature upholstered sides and are offered with ash or walnut veneer, laminate, Corian, and Fenix top surfaces.

See the full Almeya Series at arcadiacontract.com.

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Museum heists on the rise: are newly introduced criminal markets, motives and tactics evolving?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Europol’s warning that museum thefts are becoming more violent and frequent could hardly have been better timed.
  • Published on 24 August, its report, Changing Tactics, Changing Targets: The Evolving Nature of Museum Heists, was followed within days by a string of high-profile thefts.
  • “We have observed a clear and steep increase in the number of museum robbery cases since around 2022/2023,” indicates Jean-Yves Goriou, the head of the EU Organised Crime Unit, within Europol’s European Serious and Organised Crime Centre (ESOCC).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Europol’s warning that museum thefts are becoming more violent and frequent could hardly have been better timed.

Published on 24 August, its report, Changing Tactics, Changing Targets: The Evolving Nature of Museum Heists, was followed within days by a string of high-profile thefts. On 27 August thieves stole a “priceless” Bronze Age hoard from Spain’s Museum of Villena; the same day a robbery at Vienna’s Museum of Applied Arts netted a diamond necklace worth several million euros. On 8 September thieves broke into the Musée Renoir on the French Riviera, with two works by the artist still missing.

“We have observed a clear and steep increase in the number of museum robbery cases since around 2022/2023,” indicates Jean-Yves Goriou, the head of the EU Organised Crime Unit, within Europol’s European Serious and Organised Crime Centre (ESOCC). Precious metals and stones, as well as Chinese cultural artefacts are identified in the report as increasingly popular targets, a trend which the report argues can be attributed to the objects’ high financial value.

Recent findings suggest that “Some buyers in China will bid on these objects—sometimes to astronomical levels—but when they cannot acquire them legitimately, there appears to be a market for stolen Chinese treasures,” says Christopher Marinello, the founder and chief executive of Art Recovery International. He disagrees however, with the report’s claim that they “are likely to be easily sold on the art market”, arguing that “there are plenty of regulations on the books, many of which place significant burdens on honest dealers. The real problem, in my view, is the lack of effective enforcement of those regulations.”.

The concentration and visibility of attacks, particularly against museums holding exceptionally valuable jewellery and precious metals, certainly feels prominent on the public agenda—boosted perhaps by the recent anniversary of the 2025 heist of €88m worth of jewels from the Musée du Louvre in Paris.

However, given that many museum thefts have historically remained unreported—often due to embarrassment or to prevent highlighting security vulnerabilities—“the lack of substantial consistent data has long made it a challenge to establish a workable sample size”, claims Julian Radcliffe, the director of the Art Loss Register.

It has been revealed that “In the sense of volume of crimes [against museums], there’s not been a change,” claims Robert Read, the head of art and private clients at Hiscox insurance. He adds that around 50% of insurance claims continue to stem from accidental damage but adds that there does appear to be a shifting set of motivations at play. “Whereas financial value has long been understood as the key driver of such crimes, there is a sense that items could be being stolen to order, used as collateral, or even just to embarrass public institutions or governments,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that europol’s research describes a shift from the “traditional trafficker” towards an “emerging aggressor”. The former is characterised as a specialist, non-violent offender operating within a structured criminal network focused on cultural property. The latter is an ad hoc and decentralised perpetrator, prepared to use high-risk violence and operate across criminal markets, rather than concentrating exclusively on cultural property.

“A lot of these trends [in the Europol report] are not fresh, but they’re arguably occurring on a more pronounced or regular scale,” says Julian Radcliffe.

Certainly, the possibility of items being stolen to order by organised networks and with an eye on art market trends (notably the surge in demand for Chinese antiquities) has drifted in and out of public debate over museum thefts before. In 2016, for example, members of an organised gang were jailed for £57m worth of Chinese and rhino horn thefts from several UK museums and auction houses. Similarly, there is established understanding that the illicit trade in antiquities can involve networks spanning multiple types of criminality.

Breaking: WHEN

📅 16 Dec 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Identitydesigned

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information.
  • Sources indicate that the conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown.
  • In a recent development, traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information. They came to us to conceive a brand that could balance credibility and compassion in equal measure. One that felt just as comfortable in a trusted doctor’s office as the shiny shelves of a global beauty store.

Sources indicate that the conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown. But with all that focus on the fear-inducing countdown, there’s not a lot of helpful talk — about how fertility works, the proactive steps we can take to improve it, or why the biological clock is an outdated trope. That’s where WHEN comes in — a fertility medtech firm on a mission to ensure no one with ovaries is left wondering about them.

In a recent development, traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise. But this narrow focus has resulted in a category that feels overly clinical and sometimes cold, losing sight of the real people at the heart of it all. We saw an opportunity to create something that balanced the two — trust and credibility, with warmth and humanity. A direct-to-consumer lifestyle brand built on deep medical experience that felt equally at home in a retail environment.

Industry observers note that fertility is, understandably, incredibly personal and seldom discussed. To get to the heart of the concern, our friends at VML conducted a series of focus groups, one-on-one interviews and stakeholder research. Because in failing to talk about it, we’re failing to give people the information they need at the right time. People are proactive about pap smears, mammograms, skin checks, sexual health tests—all considered lead indicators that look ahead to impact the future. But fertility is measured as a lag indicator, only measured once it’s more difficult to affect the outcome.

Without jumping through costly medical hoops, there is no accessible way for people to know what’s happening inside their very own bodies without a referral. The medical industry is not set up to provide this kind of information proactively, which can make people feel blocked. And when it comes to fertility, information is power.

It has been revealed that given WHEN is the first of its kind in Australia, care needed to be taken to communicate the importance and impact of its service. Credible medical expertise was a leading reason to believe. But we also knew people needed to hear the real stories behind the brand to build trust in something so newly introduced. Striking the balance was critical.

The result is a visual and verbal system that blends emotion with science, expression with information. Designed to showcase fertility stories, expert advice and the endless questions we ask ourselves, the brand moves seamlessly from packaging to print, retail stores to social media.

Recent findings suggest that the WHEN wordmark sits at the heart of the visual identity. Clear and confident, it anchors the brand as a dependable figure in the health and medical space. Paired with an organic cell shape that reacts to the world around it, the wordmark and logoform are a perfect foil to the other. Together, they represent standing strong amid the ever-changing nature of life.

Sources indicate that WHEN’s typeface is ABC Diatype. It’s used for everything — from wordmark to body copy. Chosen for its modernity and scientific edge, it brings calm and clarity to everything we say. Paired with a colour palette of lemon and neutrals, the identity feels light and warm against an industry so often cold and clinical.

Sources indicate that an notable first touchpoint was the at-home testing kit — the Egg Count Check. The kit is split into three sections: Prepare, Collect, and Send. We designed the packaging experience to follow the same logical structure, ensuring the steps were simple to follow and easy to use.

Inspired by the sleek aesthetic of our favourite tech brands, the kit’s box takes a rigid form with special attention paid to premium print finishes. We also created a custom instruction booklet to guide the user through the process, designed and illustrated in-house.

Our primary photography style uses intimate portraits and close crops to focus on the subject’s internal thoughts and feelings. We aim to capture moments that feel like a natural extension of everyday life, empowering and relatable in their familiarity. As a secondary style, we splice natural textures and fluid forms with our portraits, like fragments of memory telling the story of a person’s inner world.

It has been revealed that to further enhance this sense of intimacy, a series of icons were developed to capture the different states of mind one might feel around this sensitive and personal topic. Following the same visual language as the logo, these icons add flexibility and expression to the brand, especially when used with the intimate portraiture.

Sources indicate that the brand name itself is a question — when? But it’s also a statement of intent. We worked with copywriter Amy Scott to develop a verbal concept exploring the idea of an inner monologue, giving voice to the questions we ask ourselves but perhaps never verbalise. The brand speaks as an empathetic expert, both insightful and inclusive. By creating space for open conversation and asking the questions people ask themselves, we show no matter where they’re at in their fertility journey, they’re not alone.

WHEN doesn’t only set to change fertility testing, but to also facilitate an aspirational platform that aims to drive community and empowering conversation around fertility. The brand was crafted to grow into a multidimensional platform for fertility information access and support. We helped design the first step of this journey through WHEN Matters — a curated blog for sharing real fertility stories and credible medical expertise to ensure no one with ovaries was left feeling alone on their journey.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (803 w)

Industry News: Group biography follows Lee Miller, Pablo Picasso and friends on holiday in the South of France

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group biography balances between a choir and a cacophony.
  • Recent findings suggest that the individuals gathered in the Hotel Vaste Horizon in the French village of Mougins formed the chain of couples constituting this community: Eileen Agar and Joseph Bard, Nusch and Paul Éluard, Ady Fidelin and Man Ray, Dora Maar and Pablo Picasso, Lee Miller and Roland Penrose.
  • Recent findings suggest that from this carefree and creative escape, Thomasson’s narrative plunges its participants into the war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group biography balances between a choir and a cacophony. Each person lies at the heart of a network, opening the potential for an exponential chain of many walk-on parts. Rooted in the photographs of what author Anna Thomasson rightly terms the “fleeting community” of a late summer holiday in 1937, A Vast Horizon succeeds remarkably in marshalling a complex tapestry of egos, events, ideals and disappointments.

Recent findings suggest that the individuals gathered in the Hotel Vaste Horizon in the French village of Mougins formed the chain of couples constituting this community: Eileen Agar and Joseph Bard, Nusch and Paul Éluard, Ady Fidelin and Man Ray, Dora Maar and Pablo Picasso, Lee Miller and Roland Penrose. They were drawn to the South of France by their inter-linked friendships and by “le peintre soleil”, Agar’s witty characterisation of Picasso. As Picasso urged everyone to work, half the witnesses took photographs. Maar, Man Ray and Miller were the relaxing professionals; snapshots were added by Agar and Penrose. Thomasson has searched through this rich, if scattered visual archive of a moment through which photography (as Roland Barthes recognised in Camera Lucida) “mechanically repeats what could never be repeated existentially”. Their hedonism caught in this moment defied the political instability and totalitarianism, with civil war already a year old in Spain.

Recent findings suggest that from this carefree and creative escape, Thomasson’s narrative plunges its participants into the war. For each of them it constituted a restructuring of values—not as hoped for by the Surrealists, but as enforced by the destructive triumphalism of Nazi extremism. Here the account turns to Paul Éluard’s transformation of a love poem for Nusch into a litany for “liberty” that captured the spirit of resistance (copies were even dropped over Occupied France by the RAF). Equally powerful was Miller’s reportage of the savagery of combat and, eventually, the revelations of the concentration camps. In this way, the book touches upon the transience of bodies captured in photography: those at Hotel Vaste Horizon were willingly posed for the camera and exchanged in partnerships, before growing fragile through wartime deprivation.

It has been revealed that there was no reciprocal gathering in the post-war period. As a result, Thomasson traces the endgames, as each of the participants ages in varying degrees of dignity, creativity and despair. Those bodies displayed on the beach in southern France become the distant, optimistic opposite to the tragic, haunting corpses of Buchenwald; it is little wonder that Miller, the photographer in both cases, would never fully recover from the experience of witnessing such deliberate inhumanity.

Picnic of stars: Lee Miller’s 1937 photo of (left to right) Nusch and Paul Éluard, Roland Penrose, Man Ray and Ady Fidelin.

Recent findings suggest that while the lives of many of these central figures are, to varying degrees, familiar—from autobiographies (Agar, Man Ray, Penrose) and biographies (Éluard, Miller, Picasso)—Thomasson’s synthesis draws on recent research and extensive reading. A particular strength is the rebalancing of longstanding gender biases and assumptions. The repositioning of Ady Fidelin, the double-marginalised Guadeloupean woman, is especially timely; drawing on fresh scholarship, she is given greater presence and somewhat rescued from simply being Man Ray’s model. Nusch Éluard is also brought more sharply into focus. Substantial traces of these women’s own voices remain to be found, however, confining them to an unknowability ascribed to their devotion to their partners, although this may be overstated in the suggestion that, in 1946, Nusch Éluard “died in the service of Paul [Éluard]’s pursuit of freedom”.

Sources indicate that late on Thomasson cites Emily Dickinson’s belief that veracity is “more affecting, if told indirectly”. This emerges as a foundational conceit in a volume inspired by photographs but in which only four are reproduced. Instead of showing, the author presents often highly evocative descriptions of what she sees in a wide range of images that the reader is not shown. This is a surprising decision for a narrative stimulated, as we are told, by the author being drawn into “their distant world by their photographs”.

Recent findings suggest that with such a limitation on images, the book’s cover photograph assumes disproportionate significance. Where the British edition favours Agar’s photograph of Maar, Picasso and the Éluards at Juan-les-Pins, Miller’s picnic photograph of “half-naked women sitting among fully clothed men”—the jarring nature of which introduces the whole narrative—appears on the cover of the US edition. Although unaltered when reproduced inside the volume, on the cover the half-naked torsos are rather ineptly airbrushed. That the publishers chose to manipulate a famous 90-year-old image seems an unfortunate undermining of an otherwise compelling narrative of artists embracing freedom before disaster struck.

ª A Vast Horizon: Artists and Lovers, Freedom and War, by Anna Thomasson, published by Pegasus Books, 304pp, 4 b/w reproductions, $29.95 (hb), 7 July.

OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made?
  • Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.
  • “Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the fresh Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

The architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” says Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

In the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

According to recent reports, the store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into fresh objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” says Gianotten.

According to recent reports, designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

According to recent reports, “We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving newly introduced value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”.

At the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

Murrye Bernard is an architect-turned-writer covering architecture, interiors, product design, and sustainability. A registered architect, she has written for Architect, Architectural Record, Metropolis, Hospitality Design, Texas Architect, Green Building Advisor, and The Architect's Newspaper. She previously served as managing editor of Contract magazine and enjoys exploring the intersection of design, materials, and culture.
