📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer. He specializes in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue, TailwindCSS, and BootStrap, with a track record of … More about Gabriel ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor? You replace ResizeObserver with a container query, the diff is mostly red, and everyone approves it before lunch.

This was what it looked like before you made the change:.

See the Pen [demo (before PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVJq) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Then, a week later, a card on the dashboard has vanished. A heading has grown on tablets for no reason anyone can explain. The spacing inside a comment is off.

See the Pen [demo (after PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/gbmBopp) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

None of these bugs are in the few lines you wrote. All of them arrived with those few lines of CSS.

According to recent reports, in my last article on how CSS is growing smarter, I left a few questions hanging at the end, including: What happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, and how do we debug conditional styles without a clear view of what triggered them? This article is my attempt to answer these two questions.

In a recent development, I think it’s worth saying clearly that I am not saying modern CSS is bad. What I am saying is that:.

A CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about if you don’t understand how it relates to existing code, be it CSS or JavaScript.

Think of a newly introduced CSS feature as a new tenant moving into a shared apartment. The tenant may be quiet and tidy, but they still share a kitchen with everyone who already lives there. In that case, CSS is now roommates with JavaScript, the component’s layout, the CSS Cascade, and the browser’s rendering engine. The apartment’s stability depends less on the tenant and more on how they get along with one another.

That gives us two different things to measure, and a diff only indicates the first one:.

I am not the only one thinking about this. In April 2026, Igor Roztropiński published an essay titled “Modern Frontend Complexity: essential or accidental?” asking:.

Recent findings suggest that the essay landed on r/programming, where the thread has drawn 80-plus comments and the replies pull in two directions. One of the most upvoted comments, from a user named Kwantuum, pushes back on the whole genre:.

Another commenter, kayinfire, takes the other side, arguing that “there are tons of scenarios where a front-end framework introduces more accidental complexity than it’s worth.” They say this a few replies later:.

I think both commenters are on to something, and this article lives in the gap between the two. Yes, CSS has improved in the last several years. And yes, “less” CSS on paper is not automatically “less” complexity in practice. That mentioned, my claim is narrower. A native feature only reduces complexity when it actually replaces what was there before and doesn’t disrupt the calm state of everything else it interacts with.

Let’s meet the housemates in our metaphorical apartment, one scenario at a time.

Recent findings suggest that the first housemate is JavaScript, and the trouble starts when the old tenant never quite moves out. Here is a card that switches to a two-column layout when it has enough room. The original version uses a ResizeObserver to toggle a class:.

With CSS Container Queries, we need no script at all and can simplify our selectors at the same time:.

It has been revealed that lovely. Now, here’s the thing: migrations rarely happen in one clean sweep. The pull request adds the @container rule and removes the .card--wide .card__body rule. The observer survives because it is registered in another file. The .card--wide .card__title rule survives because nobody searched for the class. Nothing looks broken, because both implementations agree on 480px. Then a designer asks to move the breakpoint to 600px, and a developer updates the only place they know about: the @container rule.

See the Pen [Scenario 1: The Behaviour With Two Owners [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/ZYeqvpx) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Between 480px and 600px, the card now has a single-column body and a wide-layout title. Nobody wrote that state. To find it, you need to know that the layout has two owners and read both of them.

The same trap comes in other shapes:.

It has been revealed that CSS and JavaScript can happily share a component. What they cannot share is the component’s behavior. So, instead of having a silent fight over a component’s behavior, check first. Know all the contending parties, then split the work.

Sources indicate that and when you’re done migrating, you have to finish the job: delete the observer, the class, and every selector that mentions the class. Otherwise, you may wind up with a tenant who simply refuses to move out.

It has been revealed that back in 2023, I wrote about how block formatting contexts solve float challenges. Back then, creating a block formatting context was something we did on purpose. Today, you can create one without meaning to. When we declare container-type: inline-size, we think we are saying, “let my children query my width.” The browser hears quite a bit more. This is the second housemate, the layout around the component, and our upcoming tenant who just asked for one shelf has ended up rearranging the living room.

According to MDN’s container-type reference, the value “applies style and inline-size containment to the element.” And MDN’s guide to block formatting contexts lists “query containers (elements where container-type isn’t normal)” among the CSS styles that create one. An element that establishes a new block formatting context will, in MDN’s words:.

In a recent development, that means one declaration can change three layout behaviors that have nothing to do with queries, plus a fourth that comes from inline-size containment. I built a demo where each “before” and “after” pair differs by only that one declaration.

See the Pen [Scenario 2: The Card That Vanished [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/dPvgJpB) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Sources indicate that A paragraph with margin-bottom: 16px sits above the card, and the card’s heading has margin-top: 24px. Before the change, the heading’s margin collapsed through the top of the card and merged with the paragraph’s margin, leaving a 24px gap. Afterward, the margin remained trapped inside the card. The two margins now add up to 40px, and the card grows from 30px to 54px tall.

The card follows a floated image. Before the change, the card’s box ran behind the float and its text wrapped around the image. Afterward, the whole card sits beside the float; it starts 120px further in (the width of the image) and is 120px narrower.

This is the one that makes cards vanish. Inline-size containment stops an element from taking its width from its contents. MDN has a nice, succinct explanation:.

In the last demo, three tag-sized cards sit in a flex row and measure roughly 74px, 96px, and 114px, respectively. If we add container-type: inline-size, then all three measure 0px. I got the same 0px result when the card was displayed inline-block, floated, set to a width: fit-content box, was an align-items: flex-start child of a column flex container, and when it was an item in an auto grid track. A plain block-level card retains its full width because its width is determined by its parent rather than its contents.

Recent findings suggest that in isolation, the card is a block that fills its parent. In reality, it is a flex item, follows a float, or sits under a paragraph whose margin it used to absorb.

Before you add container-type to an element, ask yourself the following three questions:.

Answering these will help prevent a housemate from completely changing the furniture layout right from under you.

Industry observers note that the third housemate is the CSS Cascade. Every shared apartment has house rules about who gets the last word, and a fresh tenant can arrive with more say than anyone expected.

In a recent development, the :has() selector and native nesting let us write short selectors in CSS. But short selectors can match more and weigh more than they appear.

In a recent development, say we want to remove paragraph margins from card components that have a hero image. This might look like it does the job:.

See the Pen [Scenario 3: The Selector That Reached Too Far [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/pvexpRd) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

This card has no hero image. Yet every paragraph in it loses its margin.

If you inspect the comment’s paragraph in DevTools and look at the “Styles” pane, you will find two culprits:.

Recent findings suggest that it could get even more complex and difficult to catch because the state changes at runtime. Let’s say a user posts a comment that includes an avatar. The body text of the card above it loses its spacing. Good luck reproducing that from a bug report that says “spacing looks off sometimes.”.

The fix is to constrain the selector with child combinators:.

This helps the selector get more specific about what it is yelling about.

Native nesting has the same habit. MDN’s guide to nesting and specificity claims the & selector takes “the largest specificity in the associated selector list,” exactly like :is(). Look at this adaptation of MDN’s example:.

A .button link inside a .card is blue, even though the #featured ID is nowhere near it. The usual reaction is a more specific .button rule, then an exception to that rule. Before you know it, you are in a war of specificity you never knew you had declared.

The way out is to keep the selector list and drop its weight by wrapping it in :where():.

Plain links inside a card are still blue, and the .button link is red again. Again, another way to quiet the loud housemate.

Sources indicate that don’t be fooled into thinking specificity is the whole story. MDN’s introduction to the cascade puts origin, importance, and cascade layers ahead of specificity, and notes that “normal layered styles have less precedence than normal unlayered styles.” In my test, a layered rule with a specificity of 0-4-0 lost to an unlayered .title (0-1-0). So if your new component styles go into @layer components while the legacy stylesheet stays unlayered, the legacy rule wins every conflict, however carefully you wrote the new one. The exception is when the !vital keyword is used, because it actually reverses the cascade order.

Sources indicate that miriam Suzanne’s original proposal for cascade layers describes exactly the pain layers were meant to remove: having to “be very careful with matching specificity to layer.” Layers do remove it, but only when the rules on both sides of the conflict are layered. A half-layered codebase just gives you one more ordering to keep in your head.

Industry observers note that none of these battles started with :has() or nesting. In an r/webdev thread titled “CSS-in-JS: What’s the biggest performance drop you actually felt?”, one of the most upvoted answers isn’t about performance at all. It is about the cascade:.

In a recent development, this is about the “order of appearance,” which is the last step in the cascade that ends up deciding a conflict nobody knew existed. Another commenter in the subreddit adds that the injected styles can land in a different order in development and production builds: “Who doesn’t love debugging something that works locally but not in prod.”.

Industry observers note that not everyone in the thread agrees on who is to blame. TheThirdRace replies, “It’s a coding issue, not a technology issue.”.

It has been revealed that I think both are right, and that is exactly the point. CSS-in-JS is a different technology from the native features we are looking at, so take this as a neighboring example, not as proof. But the shape of the problem is the same: the tool did what it promised, and the trouble arose from how it complied with the existing rules.

Industry observers note that “We moved it to CSS, so it’s faster now.” You have probably heard this in a code review, and maybe said it yourself. In my last article, I warned that it isn’t always the case. Let’s test it.

Moving a behavior from JavaScript to CSS changes who does the work. It doesn’t tell you how much work there is. The last housemate, the browser’s rendering engine, is the one who gets the bill. Everyone in the apartment shares it, and nobody looks at it after the move.

Take :has() as an example. Browser vendors were worried about its cost from the start. In a CSS Working Group issue about :has() restrictions, Emilio Cobos Álvarez noted that implementations wanted to ship it with limitations “in order to prevent performance footguns and complexity.” Today, MDN’s :has() page has a whole section on performance with two pieces of advice:.

In a recent development, I wanted numbers, so I built a list with 5,000 rows. The test toggles an .is-selected class on the same row 300 times, so the row’s selected state changes on every toggle, and forces a style and layout update each time. I ran it in Chrome 153 on a Mac in October 2026, and recorded a trace in DevTools to count how many elements each toggle restyles.

See the Pen [Scenario 4: The Rewrite Nobody Measured [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVgP) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

There are two lessons in that table.

First, the “bad” selector was fine. Rule 2 is exactly the shape MDN warns against: a :has() anchored to body. It cost about a millisecond and a half more than the script, and it restyled a single element, the toolbar. A frame at 60Hz lasts 16.7ms, so I would take that trade for deleting an event handler any day.

It has been revealed that second, two harmless rules were not harmless together. Rule 3 styles the rows, and its :has() condition remains unchanged throughout the test. On its own, it costs nothing measurable. Put it in the same stylesheet as the second rule instead, and every toggle restyles all 5,000 rows plus the toolbar. That is about what it costs a script to restyle every row on purpose.

Let’s keep this in proportion. Since 7ms still fits inside a frame, nobody would notice it on this page. However, the browser is now restyling 5,001 elements to change just one, and neither rule says so. Also, the cost grows with the list. When I set the demo to 20,000 rows, the two rules together restyled 20,001 elements and took about 31ms per toggle, which is nearly two frames.

I can tell you what Chrome does here, but not why. Changing .is-selected on one row restyles every element that the other :has() rule targets, even though that rule never mentions .is-selected and its result never changes. I have filed this with the Chromium team as an problem, with a reduced test case, and I only tested Chrome. Whatever the cause, neither rule looks suspicious in a code review, and the cost applies only when both are met.

That is system complexity in a single table. And please take the pattern from it, not the numbers: this is one page, one browser, and one machine.

The same goes for animation. The animation guide on web.dev recommends restricting animations to opacity and transform where possible, and warns that “an animation that moves an element using something other than transform is likely to be slow.” MDN’s CSS performance guide lists the properties that trigger layout when animated, such as width, height, margin, top, and left. A CSS transition on left runs layout on every frame, while a JavaScript animation of transform skips it. The property determines the cost, regardless of which language you write it in.

It has been revealed that to be fair, CSS often wins. A script that reads layout, writes styles, and reads layout again forces the browser to do layout several times in one frame, and a container query hands that whole job to the browser. But that win is something you can measure, so measure it:.

According to recent reports, each of these scenarios is small on its own. The trouble is that a real migration could hit all four scenarios at once. You have already seen three of them. They are the three bugs in the “after” demo at the top of this article. Add a long list, and you get the fourth. One move-in, four housemates disturbed.

It has been revealed that A team replaces a card’s JavaScript-driven responsive layout with a container query and :has(). The pull request adds twelve lines of CSS, deletes one script, and misses another. Within a month, three bug reports land, and there’s a chance a performance trace turns up as the fourth problem:.

Sources indicate that none of these reports means that container queries or :has() were the wrong choice. Each bug lives in the meeting point between the new CSS and the system it moved into. Still, one small pull request has sent a developer through the JavaScript, the page layout, the cascade, and the profiler.

According to recent reports, and the way out is not a return to JavaScript. Here is the same page once more, fixed.

See the Pen [demo (fixed PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/wBJYpPJ) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It still uses a container query and :has(), with three changes:.

Sources indicate that this gap between a clean start and a real codebase shows up in the same r/webdev thread. The person who started it, JRM_Insights, opens with an observation that could describe any of our four scenarios:.

Further down, mq2thez describes moving an old CSS-in-JS codebase to a newer pattern: “In isolation or greenfield maybe it wouldn’t be a huge issue,” but in practice, it meant rewriting “whole component trees.” TheThirdRace, who had been defending the technology, answers that they had only ever evaluated it “from a greenfield project perspective,” and that it was “very enlightening to see this through the lens of a spaghetti CSS migration.”.

That is the honest version of this whole article.

Recent findings suggest that most of what we read about a newly introduced feature is written from the greenfield perspective. Most of what we ship is a migration.

Before you replace JavaScript with a modern CSS feature, or adopt one in an existing codebase, answer these six questions. Think of them as the conversation to have with the housemates before the new tenant gets a key. I suggest putting the answers right in the pull request description.

According to recent reports, modern CSS is great and a huge improvement to styling as a whole. In particular, container queries and :has() let us express things that used to need a script, a dependency, or a hack. But a latest capability does not hand us a simpler system by default. In every scenario we looked at, the new tenant did something that didn’t sit well with others, and that was because nobody introduced them to the housemates’ ways of doing things. We get a simpler system when the new rule has one clear owner, a scope we have checked, a place in the cascade we chose on purpose, and numbers showing it helped.

In a recent development, so, the next time a pull request deletes more than it adds, enjoy the red lines. Then ask where the complexity went, and run the six questions. If you can’t answer one of them, the migration isn’t finished yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.

According to recent reports, dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds. In the Bistro night scene, standard three.js under WebGL leaves the cobblestones cool and flat, with a blown-out white hotspot around the round shop sign. Even with WebGPU and SSGI turned on, the lamp glare stays harsh and the pavement loses multi-bounce warmth. Slide the divider across to ThreeRT, and warm golden light spills from the shop window across the facade while overhead string lights tint the street in their own colors.

It has been revealed that the Zero-Day sci-fi corridor shows an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline. On the three.js side, ceiling pipes and glossy floors pick up heavy speckle noise, and unlit industrial housings sink into dark blue shadows. ThreeRT keeps those white and grey panels legible through soft indirect bounce light from tiny amber emitters. It doesn't rely on light probes or baked maps, so moving the camera at 60 fps never breaks the reflections of off-screen geometry.

That matters for the future of ray tracing in the browser. Today, ThreeRT runs its Rust and wgpu path tracer inside a native client while exposing a familiar three.js-style TypeScript API. The same scene code still runs as plain three.js in any browser or WebView, which gives developers one codebase across both worlds. As WebGPU hardware ray tracing matures on the web, that gap is closing fast.

You can see the range in the project gallery, from the OpenStrikeRT foundry hall where a furnace lights the surrounding concrete, to smaller studies like Jeweller's Window, Daylight Home, and Boutique Showroom. Each surface reacts to real emitters instead of faked ambient fill. See the full project on ThreeRTâs website.

British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum extend loan of Asante regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Ghana

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Asante regalia gold objects on loan from the British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) will remain on show in Kumasi, Ghana until 2030 following the extension of loan agreements by the two UK museums. The British Museum has loaned 15 objects while the V&A lent 17 pieces, almost all of which were looted during military operations in the late 19th century.

The British Museum and the V&A signed a loan agreement in 2024 with Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the 16th Asantehene (King of the Asante), to return the gold regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, the historic capital of what was then the Asante (Ashanti) empire. The loans will be renewed for a further three years at the end of the current term in April 2027. The two UK museums are legally unable to deaccession so the objects are being returned as long-term loans.

It has been revealed that “The rollover of the loan agreement was always likely and from both the British Museum’s and Manhyia Palace Museum’s point of view, this has been a successful partnership with increased visitors, training and expansion at Manhyia. There is nonetheless enduring frustration from many in Ghana, both in Asante and beyond, that this is only a loan,” indicates Barnaby Phillips, author of The African Kingdom of Gold: Britain and the Asante Treasure.

The loan renewal announcement followed a recent visit to Kumasi by Nicholas Cullinan, the director of the British Museum, following an invitation by the Asantehene.

In a recent development, the gold regalia associated with the Asante royal court is on display in the Manhyia Palace Museum's Homecoming exhibition. Items shown include a small gold ornament in the form of a lute-harp (sankuo), one of the cast gold objects presented in 1817 to British diplomat Thomas Bowdich during his trip to Kumasi.

Recent findings suggest that “The British Museum has about 220 pieces of Asante gold regalia and the Manhyia Palace Museum has been involved in the selection of objects [for loan]. There has been considerable input regarding what goes back to Ghana,” adds Phillips.

The idea of a loans deal, first discussed in the 1970s, was revived when the Asantehene visited London in May 2023 to attend the coronation of King Charles III.
